rationale: Direct evidence from systematic cohort assessments confirms that global psychomotor developmental delay (HP:0001263) is not an invariant feature of NKX6-2-related spastic ataxia type 8 (SPAX8). Instead, the clinical presentation exhibits a bifurcated spectrum: severe neonatal/early-infantile onset cases typically present with severe early psychomotor delay, lack of milestone acquisition, and early demise, whereas childhood-onset cases can attain normal early developmental motor milestones within the first year of life before developing progressive spastic ataxia and cerebellar atrophy.

evidence.text: Analysis of combined cohorts showed that patients with neonatal-onset NKX6-2-related disorder have a statistically significant higher frequency of global psychomotor developmental delay compared to later-onset groups, defining a spectrum ranging from neonatal onset with global psychomotor delay to childhood onset with a predominantly motor spastic-ataxia phenotype.

source.title: Genetic and phenotypic characterization of NKX6‐2‐related spastic ataxia and hypomyelination
source.quote: The neonatal-onset group has a statistically significant higher frequency of global psychomotor developmental delay (red) compared with the other two groups (onset from 2 months ... Our data reveal a phenotype spectrum with neonatal onset, global psychomotor delay and worse prognosis at the severe end and a childhood onset with mainly motor phenotype at the milder end.

source.quote: At the milder end of the spectrum is normal achievement of early motor milestones in the first year of life followed by slowly progressive complex spastic ataxia with pyramidal findings (spasticity with increased muscle tone and difficulty with gait and fine motor coordination) and cerebellar findings ... with loss of developmental milestones.

evidence.text: Initial identification of NKX6-2 disease established that affected members from two families had childhood-onset spastic ataxia with very slow progression, surviving into their 30s and 40s with predominant ataxia and cerebellar atrophy rather than early neonatal/infantile developmental arrest.

source.title: Mutations in NKX6-2 cause progressive spastic ataxia and hypomyelination
source.quote: Affected members of two families had childhood onset disease with very slow progression. They are still alive in their 30s and 40s and show predominant ataxia and cerebellar atrophy features on imaging. Affected members of the third family had a similar but earlier-onset presentation associated with brain hypomyelination.

evidence.text: Severe biallelic loss-of-function variants affecting the NKX6-2 homeodomain manifest with homogeneous, severe motor delays, absent head control, nystagmus, and early hypomyelination, illustrating the severe infantile pole of the condition.

source.title: Biallelic mutations in the homeodomain of NKX6-2 underlie a severe hypomyelinating leukodystrophy
source.quote: The clinical presentation was homogeneous, with four subjects having severe motor delays, nystagmus and absent head control, and one individual showing gross motor delay at the age of 6 months. All exhibited neuroimaging that was consistent with hypomyelination.

new_directions.question_text: What molecular mechanisms dictate whether an NKX6-2 variant results in severe neonatal hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with developmental arrest versus childhood-onset progressive spastic ataxia?
new_directions.rationale: Determining whether residual transcriptional repressor activity, homeodomain binding affinity differences, or alternative domain disruptions correlate strictly with age of onset and developmental delay severity.

new_directions.question_text: In childhood-onset NKX6-2 disease without initial psychomotor delay, do subtle cognitive or executive impairments emerge over decades alongside cerebellar atrophy?
new_directions.rationale: Longitudinal neuropsychological profiling of adult survivors with childhood-onset disease can clarify whether cognitive sparing is sustained long-term or undergoes late deterioration.
